source_text: CAPUT VIGESIMUM PRIMUM, De sacrosancta Trinitate. Hactenus egimus de DEO, quantum ad exsistentiam et essentiam: proximum est ut eum consideremus secundum subsistentiam suam, secundum quam Deus unus et summus est Pater aeternus, Filius ab aeterno a Patre genitus et Spiritus Sanctus procedens ab utroque, indivisa TRINITAS et impermixta UNITAS. Mysterium hoc subobscure antiqua Judaeorum Ecclesia in veteri Testamento traditum fuit, clarius vero et illustrius ab ipso LOGO, secunda Trinitatis persona, post assumptam a se carnem explanatum in N.T., in quo veteris interpretatio comprehenditur, et arcanum hoc disertius exprimitur, frequentiusque inculcatur.
english: CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE. On the most holy Trinity.

Thus far we have treated of GOD as to existence and essence: next is that we consider Him according to His subsistence, according to which the one and highest God is the eternal Father, the Son begotten from eternity from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both — undivided TRINITY and unmixed UNITY.

This mystery was handed down somewhat obscurely by the ancient Church of the Jews in the Old Testament, but more clearly and illustriously explained by the LOGOS Himself, the second person of the Trinity, after He assumed flesh, in the New Testament, in which the interpretation of the Old is contained, and this secret is more expressly set forth and more frequently inculcated.

source_text: Ejusdem profecto insaniae est, nullum Deum agnoscere et plures Deos asserere cum Zabaitis priscis, apud Averroem et Maimonidem, quibus lex Mosis potissimum opposita fuit — Deut. VI.4. Deum unum esse intelligimus, cum quod sit, ut fert imbecillitas nostra, intelligimus. Unicum enim esse necesse est, quod optimum, maximum, atque perfectissimum est. Neque summus est, qui superiorem vel parem habet. Ac duo, si pares statuantur, summus neuter erit. Quapropter haud minus execramur Cerdonis, Marcionis et Manichaeorum duos natura officioque dispares Deos invehentium delirium, quam vel Valentinianorum multiplices Aeonum foetus, vel Zabiorum aliorumque ethnicorum innumera numinum examina. At eundem personis trinum esse, arcanum est humanae rationi impervestigabile, humili fide et pietate adorandum, non curiosa aut scrupulosa sive temeritate perscrutandum. Haec enim Trinitas neque demonstrari potest a causa sua, quam nullam habet: neque ab effectibus, qui non hanc personarum distinctionem praecise et evidenter, sed id tantum quod cuilibet personae competit, declarant. Quicquid vero de hoc arcano discere licet, id ex Dei verbo discendum, moduloque divinae hujus revelationis pie acquiescendum est.
english: It is indeed of the same madness to acknowledge no God and to assert many gods with the ancient Sabaeans, in Averroes and Maimonides, to whom Moses law was chiefly opposed — Deuteronomy 6:4. We understand God to be one when we understand that He is, as our weakness bears. For that must be unique which is best, greatest, and most perfect. Nor is he highest who has a superior or equal. And if two are set as equals, neither will be highest.

Therefore we no less execrate the delirium of Cerdo, Marcion, and the Manichees bringing in two gods unequal in nature and office, than either the Valentinians multiple offspring of Aeons, or the Sabaeans and other pagans innumerable swarms of deities. But that the same is threefold in persons is a secret unsearchable to human reason, to be adored with humble faith and piety, not searched with curious or scrupulous rashness.

For this Trinity can neither be demonstrated from its cause, which it has none, nor from effects, which do not declare this distinction of persons precisely and evidently, but only what belongs to each person. But whatever may be learned of this secret is to be learned from Gods word, and one must piously rest in the measure of this divine revelation.

source_text: Quae enim apud Trismegistum, Platonem, Plotinum aliosque Platonicos philosophos de tribus principiis, mente, verbo et spiritu leguntur, aliena prorsus sunt ab hoc arcano, quia isti tres hypostases ideoque tres Deos separatos fingunt; etsi haec illorum opinio e prisca Hebraeorum Chaldaeorumque doctrina et purae religionis reliquiis profluxisse videatur. E Scholasticis Scotus, Gandavensis, Bonaventura et alii hoc mysterium rationibus naturalibus demonstrare conantur: quos et Keckermannus noster in systemate theologico nonnihil aemulatur. Experientia vero docet, neminem de eo cogitaturum fuisse, nisi e patriarcharum familia traditio aliqua ad gentiles percrebuisset. Data autem revelatione, haud difficile est rationes adversariorum collatas dissolvere. Circa res maxime fundamentales suboriri possunt problemata quaedam minime fundamentalia, quae prisci patres si suo seculo mota fuissent, cum periculo schismatis inter ecclesias aut suscitandi aut continuandi nunquam definire tentassent — ut monet reverendissimus pater D. Joh. Davenantius episcopus Sarisburiensis. Deum esse unum in essentia, trinum in personis inter se distinctis, Filium genitum esse a Patre, Spiritum sanctum esse Patris et Filii Spiritum, hasce tres personas esse coaeternas et coaequales, merito definita sunt haec omnia inter articulos fundamentales collocata.
english: For what is read in Trismegistus, Plato, Plotinus and other Platonic philosophers concerning three principles — mind, word, and spirit — is altogether alien from this secret, because those men invent three hypostases and therefore three separate gods; though this opinion of theirs seems to have flowed from the ancient doctrine of the Hebrews and Chaldeans and remnants of pure religion.

Among the Scholastics Scotus, Gandavensis, Bonaventure and others try to demonstrate this mystery by natural reasons: whom our Keckermann in his theological system somewhat emulates. But experience teaches that no one would have thought of it unless some tradition from the patriarchal family had spread to the Gentiles. Yet once revelation is given, it is not hard to dissolve the adversaries gathered reasons.

Around the most fundamental things certain least-fundamental problems can arise, which the ancient fathers, if they had been raised in their age, would never have tried to define with the danger of stirring or continuing schism among the churches — as the most reverend father Dr. John Davenant, bishop of Salisbury, warns. That God is one in essence, threefold in persons distinct among themselves, that the Son is begotten from the Father, that the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of Father and Son, that these three persons are coeternal and coequal — all these have rightly been defined and placed among fundamental articles.

source_text: Caeterum, voce Trinitatis hic non numerum ternarium numerantem simpliciter, sed personas in una essentia distinctas significamus. Persona in Deo est hypostasis seu subsistentia individua, incommunicabilis, viva, intelligens, volens, potens, agens — Joh. V; XIV. Sunt autem tres personae, Pater, Filius et Spiritus Sanctus, non tres Dei, quia una est essentia seu deitas — Col. II.9; I Joh. V.7. Sic orthodoxi patres e voce ousia et hypostasis distinctionem constituerunt. Non sunt tres Dei, tres Domini, etc. Persona cum relationibus quibus constituuntur subsistentes sunt — Joh. XIV. Non sola tamen ratione, sed reipsa distinctae, di ratione cujusdam proprietatis et relationis.
english: Moreover, by the word Trinity here we do not signify a ternary numbering number simply, but persons distinct in one essence. A person in God is a hypostasis or individual subsistence, incommunicable, living, understanding, willing, powerful, acting — John 5; 14.

But there are three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, not three Gods, because the essence or deity is one — Colossians 2:9; 1 John 5:7. Thus the orthodox fathers established the distinction from the words ousia and hypostasis. There are not three Gods, three Lords, and so on.
Person with the relations by which they are constituted are subsistences — John 14. Yet they are distinct not by reason alone but in the thing itself, by reason of a certain property and relation.

source_text: Si solus Pater gignit, proprium est ipsi generare; si solus Spiritus sanctus procedit ac spiratur, proprium est ipsi procedere ac spirari. Ac similis in modo est inter Patrem et Filium relatio. Est autem notio nihil aliud quam proprietas seu actus notionalis, qui per synecdochen generis relationem denotat. Unde in scholis quinque in universum sunt divinarum personarum notiones, de quibus praeter scholasticos priscos et doctissimos viros Hier. Zanchium et Fr. Junium, videas theologorum Leidensium synopsin purioris theologiae, disp. VII.thes.21-24. Trinitas personarum illustrari quodammodo potest similitudinibus e libro naturae: demonstrari autem debet e solo libro Scripturae. Nam a rebus finitis ad infinitam Dei essentiam infirma nimis consequentia est, et hoc arcanum lumine naturae altius est.
english: If the Father alone begets, it is proper to Him to beget; if the Holy Spirit alone proceeds and is spirated, it is proper to Him to proceed and be spirated. And there is a similar relation in mode between Father and Son.

But a notion is nothing other than a property or notional act, which by synecdoche of the genus denotes relation. Hence in the schools there are in all five notions of the divine persons, concerning which besides the ancient scholastics and most learned men Jerome Zanchi and Franciscus Junius, see the Leiden theologians Synopsis of purer theology, disputation 7 theses 21-24.

The Trinity of persons can in some way be illustrated by likenesses from the book of nature: but it ought to be demonstrated from the book of Scripture alone. For from finite things to Gods infinite essence the consequence is too weak, and this secret is higher than natures light.

source_text: In ordine personarum generantem generato cogitando praeponimus — Matth. XXVIII.19; Joh. V.26-27. Generatio activa tribuitur Patri; generatio proprie dicta fit per communicationem totius essentiae. Recte asserimus Patrem ex se Filium genuisse: principium quod generat, Pater est; principium quo generatio fit, natura est. Hinc persona gignens et genita relationes oppositas constituunt. Trinitas personarum illustrari quodammodo potest similitudinibus e libro naturae; demonstrari autem debet e sola Scriptura. CAPUT VIGESIMUM SECUNDUM, De DEO PATRE, sequitur.
english: In the order of persons we set the begetter before the begotten in thought — Matthew 28:19; John 5:26-27. Active generation is attributed to the Father; generation properly so called comes about by communication of the whole essence.

We rightly assert that the Father has begotten the Son from Himself: the principle which begets is the Father; the principle by which generation comes about is nature. Hence the begetting and begotten person constitute opposite relations.
The Trinity of persons can in some way be illustrated by likenesses from the book of nature; but it ought to be demonstrated from Scripture alone. CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO, On GOD THE FATHER, follows.
